subsystems.name: Neural sensing
subsystems.role: reads brain activity without requiring the user to do anything.
parts: dry-contact EEG electrodes in headrests or furniture

subsystems.name: Supporting physiology
subsystems.role: cross-checks the brain signal with the rest of the body.

subsystems.name: Signal and inference layer
subsystems.role: turns noisy voltages into a real-time estimate of mental workload.
parts: feature extraction (EEG band power, evoked responses)

subsystems.name: Actuators
subsystems.role: change the room in ways people feel rather than notice.
parts: tunable LED lighting (dimming and colour temperature)
active noise control and sound masking

subsystems.name: Control loop
subsystems.role: decides when and how much to adjust.
parts: hysteresis and rate limits to avoid flicker

subsystems.name: Privacy and consent layer
subsystems.role: keeps neural data on-site and under the user's control.

buildSteps.title: Define what is being measured
buildSteps.detail: Pick a validated index of cognitive load and prove it moves with task difficulty, using standard tasks and a workload questionnaire such as the NASA Task Load Index.

buildSteps.title: Build comfortable, long-wear sensing
buildSteps.detail: Dry electrodes must work through hair or be hidden in a headrest, and stay stable for hours while people move and talk.

buildSteps.title: Collect labelled training data
buildSteps.detail: Record many people doing easy and hard versions of real tasks so the system learns what high load looks like, including fatigue and stress, which look similar.

buildSteps.title: Train and calibrate the decoder
buildSteps.detail: Models are trained partly on groups and partly per person; a short calibration routine and drift correction are needed because electrode contact changes.

buildSteps.title: Instrument the room
buildSteps.detail: Install lights, speakers, seating and HVAC that can be adjusted finely and quickly, and test that the change is perceptible but not distracting.

buildSteps.title: Close the loop
buildSteps.detail: A controller maps load estimate to a room setting, with a latency budget of roughly a second, plus limits on how often it may change.

buildSteps.title: Design for safety and consent
buildSteps.detail: Add failsafes, always-on manual control, on-device processing and data-minimisation rules before anyone experiences the system.

buildSteps.title: Pilot in a real space
buildSteps.detail: Deploy in a classroom, clinic or control room alongside a control group, and measure outcomes such as task performance, stress and comfort.

buildSteps.title: Validate claims
buildSteps.detail: Regulators treat health claims strictly, so the product must separate proven effects from unsupported wellness marketing.

prerequisites.why: estimating workload from EEG without asking the user to act is demonstrated in labs, but reliability outside them is limited.
signal quality still degrades with hair, sweat and movement over a working day.
commercially deployed LED and noise-control systems give a fast, fine-grained actuator layer.
inference must run locally to keep latency and privacy acceptable.
rules for neural data in buildings — retention, consent, misuse — are largely absent.

pathway.milestone: lab studies linking measured workload to adaptive lighting or sound
pathway.unlocks: evidence that the closed loop changes anything useful.

pathway.milestone: single-room pilots in clinics or classrooms with control groups
pathway.unlocks: real-world reliability figures and user acceptance.

pathway.milestone: multi-user spaces that sense groups rather than individuals
pathway.unlocks: offices, schools and hospitals where adaptation benefits most people present.

pathway.milestone: buildings that adapt to occupants by default under clear consent rules
pathway.unlocks: environments tuned continuously for attention, rest and accessibility — provided the privacy and evidence questions are settled.
